newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space station hits cargo craft.
newsitem.headline: Russian space station hits cargo craft.

text.p: Russia's Mir space station collided on Wednesday with a cargo craft during a manual docking exercise in what mission control called "the most serious accident in recent times" involving the ageing vessel.
The three-man crew, U.S. astronaut Michael Foale and Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, were in no immediate danger but faced power problems, space officials said.

"The cosmonauts say there is a fall in the electrical supply...and as a result of the collision a hole (in the scientific module used for the docking) has developed whose size is still unclear," said mission control head Vladimir Lobachyov.

"This was the most serious accident in recent times," he told a news briefing at the mission control centre near Moscow. He said it was not yet clear what had caused the accident but added that a technical malfunction might have been at fault.
The unmanned Progress cargo craft collided at 1.20 p.m. (0920 GMT) with the Spektr scientific module attached to the main section of Mir, causing a partial loss of air pressure.
A spokesman for the U.S. space agency NASA said earlier on Wednesday that the crew had been able to seal off the damaged compartment after the collision.

The main part of the station -- in orbit for more than a decade -- was not affected by the collision but a solar battery on the Spektr may have been damaged, a Russian spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone.
A space expert who requested anonymity said damage to the solar battery could cause serious problems but declined to give details until the full picture emerged.
The RIA news agency quoted space experts as saying that the Spektr is the main carrier of solar batteries and the chief source of energy for the entire station.
Lobachyov said a commission would decide Spektr's fate and added that it might be undocked from the space station.
Progress had been travelling at a speed of six metres a second at the time of collision and the crew had tried to prevent the accident, he said.
Progress is now moving away from Mir and is expected to fall to Earth and sink into the Pacific Ocean on Friday.
The launch of the next cargo craft, set for June 27, will probably be postponed, Lobachyov said.
The crew has sufficient water and food supplies on board.
Vladimir Solovyov, responsible for flight coordination at the Korolyov centre, said an eighth of the Mir station was now temporarily out of action because of the collision.
Mir, the world's only space station, was launched in 1986 and has suffered a series of malfunctions in recent months, including a fire and a leakage of coolant.
Wednesday's manual docking was part of a training programme to help the crew cope with malfunctions.

"Cargo craft are normally docked in automatic mode but because of a string of recent failures the cosmonauts train in manual docking from time to time to polish their skills," the Russian spokeswoman said.
The crew could be returned to Earth at short notice in a Russian Soyuz escape craft kept docked to Mir at all times. NASA said there was no immediate plan to evacuate the three men.
Mir is due to be replaced by an international station called Alpha in the next few years.
